utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good morning to everyone. Madam Registrar, would you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Case number IT-98-29-T, the Prosecutor versus Stanislav Galic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Registrar. Is the Defence ready to call its next expert witness, and that's --

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Not quite, Mr. President, in the sense that we told Madam Registrar that we wished to address your Chamber for a couple of minutes, even less.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much. There are two reasons for this intervention. The first one is to try and reply to the Prosecution's worry about the transparency for this witness expert, and this is what we wanted to say to make things completely clear. An important part of the work of the expert was based upon what we call the orality. And I will explain. There have been four trips that this expert did and went to Sarajevo and to visit the sites, and for those four trips, two happened with a group of experts. These were other experts, that is, there was one expert who specialised in military matters, and then there was another expert who was specialised in forensic medicine. When they were on the site, they discussed among them informally in order to inform each other. But in all of that there was no minutes of that. There was no trace, so to speak, about information in situ, as it will be the case about a silent visit that could take in such-and-such a place. That was more or less what took place. Now, the second thing is that the expert took a number of photographs that he used for his own ends, internal ends, to be aware of the geographic situation when he was working in Belgrade or elsewhere, and these photographs were not communicated to the Prosecution. Why not? For a very simple reason: That the Prosecution themselves have photographed everything, and therefore it would have been completely redundant to communicate these photographs. However, if the Prosecution wish to have these photographs, they are at their disposal. And I have asked the expert to bring them with him. But we don't think that they are relevant -- they are necessary. And the Prosecution knows about how we've worked with the expert because one trip took place in Sarajevo with the expert and the representative of the Prosecution. I believe that was Mr. Ierace, who saw very well how these trips happened, that is, how the examination took place. Now, about the transparency, we have given everything -- we have disclosed everything. The notes that are to do with the photograph, which angle, which direction, and so on, do not seem to be sufficiently informative to be communicated. But of course, if they're necessary -- again, I've asked the expert to take his photographic references if this was necessary. This is for the first part of the intervention. For the second part of my intervention, Mr. President, we have seen and we have understood the matter -- the issue of the Chamber in terms of credibility. We do not wish to assist about credibility issues being raised, and we trust that the Trial Chamber will be careful of this matter. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I did not fully understand your last four lines, Mr. Piletta-Zanin.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] What I said, Mr. President, is that we thank -- we thank the Chamber about the position that they expressed about the way that the cross-examination was conducted on the issue of credibility, and we hope that we will not assist at the same way of treatment of the expert witness on the pretext of testing the credibility of the witness, asking him questions like they were asked yesterday, and we wanted to stress this because we believe this was one way, if it's not, that this would destabilise an expert, and we don't think that is the purpose of the exercise. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: To make it quite clear, the Chamber has expressed itself yesterday clearly that positions taken in previous writings do not as such in whatever way affect the truthfulness of a testimony given in this court under oath. At the same time, if it's done prudently, an expert witness may be confronted with earlier writings and the contents of it. I hope that that's clear for all the parties, so it's also a matter of the way in which it is done. Mr. Ierace, is there any need to respond to the first part of the --

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Mr. President, we now learn that the witness who is about to be called as an expert has been given information by persons so far unnamed, has been party to discussions on the contents of his report, or at least the background to preparing his report with persons unnamed, conversations untaped. In other words, the Prosecution is not being provided with all of the relevant material on which the witness based his opinions. I also note that even within the body of the report the -- and recent correspondence with the Defence, it is now clear that the opinions of the witness are based not only on the evidence but on statements given to him, including by persons who were not even called as witnesses. So Mr. President, I think ultimately the issue of the admissibility of this witness's evidence has to be reassessed. I'm in your hands as to whether that's done now or at the end of his evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In order to clarify for once and for all and to avoid wasting time, it is not true to say that these trips and examination took place with unmentioned persons. What I said is that they are our experts, Dr. Cavoski and so on. And they were there. There was a ballistics expert. And then there was also Mr. Radinovic and Mr. Dunjic, all experts. And these are all names of experts that we are talking about. The Prosecution cannot say that they did not know what was going on. And the fact, in order to save time -- and we've organised visits with several experts -- doesn't mean that the work that each of the experts has done would have been invalidated [Realtime transcript read in error "validated] by the fact that they were together. On the contrary. I believe that this would allow more information. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Ierace.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Mr. President, perhaps since it's now been referred to twice, I should explain what happened when my learned colleague refers to the Prosecution being aware of what was going on and being present during examinations. During a filming session of sniping incidents in September 2001, the Prosecution invited Ms. Pilipovic to attend the filmings. She attended, I think, two filmings. She appeared on the scene -- well, I think she came with us from the UN building, in separate vehicles, and was accompanied by some men. And at one of those site visits, she introduced me to the men and that was it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That's --

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: That's hardly a matter of the Prosecution being present during examinations by the Defence experts. One also wonders what a military expert had to do with -- by way of assistance with a ballistics expert. But again, I'm in your hands as to whether the admissibility of this witness's evidence is determined now on what we know, photographs undisclosed, notes undisclosed, conversations with persons still not entirely named, let alone with notes, or whether we do it at the end.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, first of all, for the transcript, I did not say "validated" but "invalidated." That's the first point. The second issue is that we cannot -- I'm sorry about the time that's passing, but the Defence cannot be reproached with wanting to look for making the most of its work by making one trip with several experts who are well known --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Piletta-Zanin, let's just stop the discussion. The most important thing for the Chamber to know is what sources of information are used by the expert. And the Chamber will at the very beginning of the expertise --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The Chamber will at the very beginning of the testimony of this expert witness try to establish what is the basis of his expertise. Of course, it's clear that even in the report, reference is made to statements unknown to the Chamber. So therefore, there's a need to know that. The Chamber does not think it to be dramatic if someone has discussed, I mean, what -- that's something that might have happened often while preparing a report, that you check with other experts, whether your theoretical position is the right one, et cetera, et cetera. So as such, we have to clearly distinguish the factual basis of the report of an expert, which is not the same as the theoretical basis for it. But the Chamber would like -- just like to be informed precisely on what happened. Ms. Pilipovic, you were the first to stand up. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour. Thank you. Good morning to everyone. Your Honour, what I wish to do is to clarify the trip to Sarajevo and also the examination, the visit of the sites by the Defence and by the experts, and when Mr. Ierace was present, if that is necessary. If it will be necessary, since I was there the whole time, I can explain. We have the video recordings, video filmings. And of course, I've had the escort from UN security, because I had asked for it for my experts. So it wasn't a very brief visit to Sarajevo. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The Chamber will put a few questions to the expert right at the beginning of the testimony, as it has been done for some experts of the Prosecution as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: And in that regard, Mr. President, might I remind you of the request yesterday that we have available to us a copy of all of the materials that the Defence provided to the expert. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. That's how I understood your request of yesterday, that at least we would know what written materials have been put to -- at the disposal of the expert witness. And that's one of the questions we'll ask him. Then Mr. Ierace, are you interested to review the photographs that, as we hear from the Defence, are taken by the -- yes. We'll then ask the expert witness to make them available because that's one of the possible sources of his report. Madam Usher, could you please escort the witness into the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I apologise. I take it that you are Dr. Kunjadic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Kunjadic, yes. Milan, yes. Doctor.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I'll put the emphasis on the first part of your name. Dr. Kunjadic, first of all, if you put on your earphones, can you hear me in a language you understand?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I can.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I take it that you prefer to give your testimony in your own language, which is what we call Bosnian/Serbian/Croatian, B/C/S?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The Rules of Procedure and Evidence require you to make a solemn declaration before giving evidence in this court. The text of that solemn declaration will be handed out to you now by the usher, and I'd like to invite you to make that solemn declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Please be seated, Dr. Kunjadic. Before you'll be examined by the parties, I've got a few questions for you. We've all read your report, and one of the things I would like to know is where you say that you have received material from the Defence, documents you say include photocopies of police reports, medical findings, written statements, do you have a full list of the material or do you have a full bundle of the material that has been put at your disposal and on the basis of which you worked while preparing your report?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] While I was doing my report, I had everything that the Defence had offered to me at my disposal, and these were videotapes. These were --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: May I stop you. I am aware the type of material that was --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- Given to you by the Defence to work on. But do you have a complete list of, for example, video A, B, C, and D, written statement of Witness E, written statement of Witness I. So we'll try to identify the exact sources you used.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] What I had -- and I have the list here. I also have the expanded so-called working expert report which I compiled before the trial. And in this expanded expert report, I also included everything that I believed to be relevant to give my expert opinion and the findings. But because this report was extremely large, considerable, I was advised to shorten it because it was -- there were also lists of documents. And what we waited for -- I was told to shorten it. And what we waited for was to receive the transcript. So I compared the transcript with the statements that I had while I was doing the first expanded report.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: But again, I do understand that you worked on it, that you received material. Do we have -- for example, if you're talking about transcripts. I take it that these are transcripts from the court proceedings here.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: But I also take it that you did not receive all the transcripts of 12 months, 13 months, that you received a selection. Therefore, we would very much like to know what exactly you received as a basis for your work. Do you have a list or do you have a --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have a selection of transcripts here. In any case, what witnesses were heard, and these transcripts were given to me by the Defence through a translator or through an interpreter, and I processed this in the summer of last year, and I compared with the previous statements that had been given to see if there were any differences. However, because I understood that there were no considerable differences, I then didn't quote them in any special way.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I didn't refer to them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I do understand. But of course it is up to the parties and also to the Chamber to see whether there are any differences and what -- if there are any differences, what the relevance is. Would you be willing to -- to provide a list of exactly those -- those transcripts you received so that the parties can check exactly what you had available when you were working and what exactly you had there to compare with earlier statements?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] From the Defence, in order to prepare today's hearing, I was given the material that I compared to the transcripts.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Is that the full set of material you received, apart from videos?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] These are statements. These are statements with the material inside, with photographs and the complete material.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, that's the material as you received it.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I received it -- I mean, I had it before, and I used it to write the first version.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I had been issued for confidentiality reasons, and then I returned it. And now when I was preparing for this hearing, I asked to have a look at it again, the sketches, the photographs, all the material that cannot be taken away.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I take it that this is the material you received and not your annotations you made. This is, may I take it, the -- did you make any annotations in this material for yourself?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: In order to give the Prosecution an opportunity to verify the basis on which the expert worked, the Prosecution should be allowed to inspect the material available. Whether it should be done now right away or during the first break is a different matter. Perhaps it -- but it should be put at the disposal for inspection to the Prosecution so that you exactly know what material the witness has received.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Mr. President, I'd seek a short adjournment -- a very short adjournment at this stage simply so that we can look through it in a cursory fashion.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: And then I would say --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: How much time would you need?

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Fifteen minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Fifteen minutes. Yes, Mr. Piletta-Zanin.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, in order for your Chamber to understand more fully why we didn't think that it was useful to hand over these photographs, perhaps you can ask the witness if he has these photographs with him and he can then submit it either to you, your Chamber, or to the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. We have been informed that you also made your own photographs of sites you have visited. Although there's not a lot about your visits on the sites in the report, would you be willing to put your photographs at the disposal of the parties as well so that they can check whether there's any information on these photographs that is of any relevance for them, either for questioning you or for the case as a whole?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As it happens, coincidentally I have these photographs because I was reminding myself about certain details from them. I didn't think that the Chamber needed them. And just like some of the notes that Professor Dunjic and myself we took in Sarajevo when we were marking from where the photographs was taken. That was on the 15th of May, 2001. We were a second time in Sarajevo, when we couldn't visit the sites at our leisure -- the incident sites at our leisure. But what we did, we tried to remark -- to observe the streets and the field and the conditions under which incidents could have happened. We visited the demarcation lines, and that's when I made a set of photographs, and I can of course submit them to be perused.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. One additional question: How did you know exactly where the demarcation lines were? Who told you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That was presented by the Defence to us.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Did you receive any maps in that respect as to where the confrontation lines --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We received a map of the city of Sarajevo, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Were the demarcation lines marked on it or ...?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The demarcation line was marked in. That was presented to us by the Defence. That's the map that we received from the Defence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Do you still have that map?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't think I have that map here. But I -- I'm not quite sure. I have a lot of material. I'll have to have a look if you wish to have it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I've seen in the report that apart from mentioning that a certain position was close to the confrontation line, without giving any further position, I don't know whether the parties would need it. But if you could find it, that would be good. So that you'll understand what the parties and what the Chamber also seeks is to establish clearly on what basis you have given your expert opinion. Mr. Ierace.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: On page 2 of the report, there's a reference to maps, plural. Perhaps it would be appropriate to ask the witness if he was given any other maps.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Was there one map or were there several maps that ...? And were these coloured maps with darker and clearer green lines and red circles, or doesn't that ring a bell to you? Because that's a type of map we've seen several times. I don't know whether these types of maps are used.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] When I was in Sarajevo, we used a map to find streets and incident sites, because at that moment we didn't know the incident sites. The sites, we only knew them exactly when the investigator came. And in six or seven incidents we were for the same time in September 2002. So when I'm talking about a map, I'm talking about a map of Sarajevo. But of course I also know about the maps where sniping incidents were marked. And I had those maps in front of me on several occasions like at the time when I consulted the Defence when Mr. Hinchliffe testified in July this year.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. That clarifies, at least, that that's also part of the material that you have seen, at least.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Ms. Pilipovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I just would like to ask you -- to ask Mr. Kunjadic also whether the video filming was done by the Defence when we were in Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Yes. You've told us about videos you've seen. Ms. Pilipovic now refers to videos taken by the Defence. Did you only see those videos, or did you also see other videos?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] When I was talking about videotapes, I meant the videotapes that the Prosecution presented. But according to my brief, there were also videotapes that were made, that is, video recordings, of incidents at the time when the investigator was there, also in September. That is, in incidents number 5, 6, 17 -- 16 and 17. We also filmed other things, because together with us there was the military expert as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Ms. Pilipovic, I do understand that the expert witness has been provided with videotapes produced by the Prosecution with -- Is there a list what videotapes you exactly have viewed or -- or all the videotapes? Have you put at the disposal of the expert witness all the videotapes or ...?

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, a precise list of video cassettes that we received from the Prosecution is precise inasmuch as all the incidents were on one videotape that the Defence received from the Prosecution in November 2001, before the trial. And the video material that the Defence filmed in September 2001, this is the video material in edited versions, that is, in shortened versions, all in -- on one tape, probably about an hour and a half duration. And to my learned colleagues I disclosed three videotapes that are directly linked to four incidents that the Defence visited the sites of together with my colleagues and filmed with the cameramen of the Defence, who was also present at those site where the cameramen of the filming crew of the Prosecution were also at those.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Has the shortened edited version of the Defence video recordings been put at the disposal of the expert, or have the -- has the full version been put at his disposal? I mean, is there any difference between what you disclosed to the Prosecution and what you gave to the expert?

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The full version. Your Honour, certain details with regard to certain incidents -- there's no difference. But from that part of the video material, I made three video cassettes, and there are four incidents on those video cassettes. The other video material has also been shown to Mr. Kunjadic, and these recordings, which I disclosed to the Prosecution, has to do with part of the material for specific incidents where that same place was filmed which was filmed by my learned colleagues. But in this case, the filming was carried out on order of the ballistics expert -- at the request of the ballistics expert.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Pilipovic, there's one question I want to be sure about: Is there any video material -- has any video material been given to the expert which has not been given to the Prosecution? That's the main question. Even if it would be one second or ten seconds or relevant or irrelevant, is there any video material given to the expert which has not been disclosed fully to the Prosecution?

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, on the video cassette that was made on that day there are perhaps certain details that the Defence filmed for itself.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Pilipovic, the question is whether any material has been given to the expert which has not been disclosed -- if you made videos for your own -- just for your own memory, for your own recollection of what you personally saw, that's a different matter. But is there any, even the smallest portion, of video which has been put -- which has been given to the expert and that has not been disclosed to the Prosecution? That's the precise question I'm putting to you.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, there is a part -- a certain part of video material on one of the video cassettes, and I think it was disclosed to the Prosecution and that has to do with the topography of Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: But you're now telling us that there was one part that was disclosed. My question was whether there was anything given to the expert which has not been given to the Prosecution. That's -- I think it's a quite simple question.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The expert has seen not one single piece of video material which has not been available to the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, that video material is accessible to the Prosecution. It's one video cassette on which the entire topography of Sarajevo was filmed. Mr. Kunjadic was present at the time too. And these three video cassettes we can be seen here, and that is connected to the incidents. I just have to check to see whether it's video cassette number 7 or 8. And the video cassette also shows the command post of General Galic, and from that video cassette last year I presented -- I showed to Mr. Indic a part that lasts for three minutes, in which you can also see the command post of the general.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Your answer is clear. There's nothing that has not been disclosed to the Prosecution that might have been used by the -- by the expert witness. Mr. Ierace.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: That may be the case, Mr. President, but this is the first time the so-called topography video has been indicated to the Prosecution as being part of the material that was shown to this witness, and it will take us a little time to locate that amongst the disclosed material from the Defence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. It at least was not quite clear what material exactly was on the basis of the report. Under the supervision of the registrar, the Prosecution will have 15 minutes from now on to check both the written sources that the witness indicated have been provided to him when he prepared his report and also to have a look at the photographs that you were so kind to put at our disposal. We'll adjourn for 15 minutes. --- Break taken at 9.43 a.m.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Ierace.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Thank you for that, Mr. President. First of all, in relation to the statements, they appear in bundles with a paper sleeve and on each sleeve is marked the incident number.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Missing are the folders for incidents 3, 4, 11, 14, and 15. That's the first problem. Secondly, whilst, of course, I haven't yet had an opportunity to go through the context -- the contents, I picked one randomly. Excuse me. Incident number 9. The report reads in part, "There is no evidence that fire had been opened from an AA machine-gun with exploding ammunition as indicated in the official police record made by the Vogosca Public Security Station officers." So I went to folder 9, and although we haven't been able to organise our language assistant at such short notice, it does appear to contain a statement by one of the witnesses, an English translation of that statement. Excuse me. And some photographs and a map but no police report. Therefore, in two respects to an unknown degree, in relation to one of those respects, it appears on the face of it that the material is incomplete. Going to the photographs, there are something like about 40 photographs. A number of the photographs appear to be general views of parts of Sarajevo which I'm able to recognise; others of buildings which I don't recognise, some of which I suspect what they may be; others of buildings, perhaps a few photographs of one building, that type of thing, that I have no idea what it is or what the significance is. We were given some notes in B/C/S. To the extent that we're able to translate those notes, the information in the notes doesn't really assist us very much as to their significance or lack of significance. Mr. Piletta-Zanin generously offered to translate for me during the break. I'm grateful for that. But I think we were able to get by sufficiently to identify the defects in that. Now, Mr. President, the danger with this is that in chief the witness may be asked about something in the photographs. We haven't had an opportunity to -- to check it out beforehand. Or even worse, the photographs might be used in re-examination, giving us even less of an opportunity.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If the photographs are of any relevance, then of course they should have been disclosed to the Prosecution or at least the Prosecution should have been notified about the existence of these photographs.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Might I respectfully interrupt.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: That is not the point that I seek to make. It's not a question of disclosure. It's a question of understanding how this witness came to his conclusions, how this material is relevant to those conclusions, whether there is other material which contributed to those conclusions. That's why, in my respectful submission, this material should have been identified in the report in a way which transparently conveys that process. So even if we had had these photographs two weeks ago, that wouldn't have been of much assistance to us without an explanation in writing from the witness explaining what they mean to him, what their relevance is. Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Piletta-Zanin.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, we can see that there's quite a lot of confusion here, no distinctions made between form and substance. If the witness does not have all the elements in his file that are necessary to him, according to the Prosecution, that would be another matter. It would be necessary to verify to see whether he was in a position to reach such-and-such a conclusion. That's another problem. It concerns the form. But the fact, Mr. President, is that all the information that was provided to this witness come from the Prosecution's file, in fact, regardless of the form, with certain minor exceptions. I will mention the photographs, the notes that I didn't offer to translate -- I offered to explain the photographs to Mr. Ierace, if he wanted me to do so. And it also concerns the topographic reports and that concerns the notes in question. Mr. President, the fact that photographs were taken is absolutely irrelevant with regard to the problem that has been raised. Given that we know that for each of these sites the Prosecution made 360-degree photographs, and even certain computer projections, and the fact that the expert wanted to take these photographs for himself in order to be able to remember the situation when he -- when he was working. It's just an indicator of good sense. It shows his professional concern with regard to his manner of carrying out his task, performing his task. It's quite simple and that's where it ends. To raise this issue is just an argument that seems to us to be quite hollow, in fact, because we all know -- we all have these sites in mind. They've been recorded, photographed, et cetera. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I'd like to make two observations: The first is that form and substance are often interrelated, so that it's not of great assistance to say that it's just a form because forms have something to do with substance. The second issue is that things are hardly ever as simple as they look at first sight. The Chamber has assisted the Prosecution as far as it stands now to give at least some insight in -- at least a more precise insight in the sources used by the expert witness. We'll ask the expert witness about 3, 4, 11, 14, and 15. I just have to -- then we should not forget that most of the conclusions of the expert tend in a direction which say since we have no bullet found, we cannot establish what the bullet was. The conclusions are very much in the negative sense. And it's for most of these conclusions there seems to be not great puzzles as to the basis on what these conclusions are drawn and those conclusions are very often drawn on the basis of the absence of certain information and the absence of reports on entry wounds, exit wounds, et cetera, et cetera. Therefore, we should now start with the examination of this expert witness. We should try to clarify those parts missing and whether on a photograph at a distance -- a photograph that might just have been used for the memory of the expert, whether it really is appearing at the distance of three or four hundred metres or not might not have that great relevance that would be a reason for great concern at this moment in this respect. Let's see where we get, and we'll first ask the missing parts of the documentation. Madam Usher, could you please escort the witness into the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please be seated. Dr. Kunjadic, the Prosecution has just gone through your material briefly, and they informed us that there seems to be no documentation on incidents 3, 4, 11, 14, and 15. Are you aware of that, and what would be the reason of the absence of those five incidents in your documentation?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't know. I had all those incidents earlier on, and I have now taken them from the Defence to remind myself of what was contained in them. I explained that. But excerpts from that material, I have it also written down in this version which I made.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Do I understand you well that you gave back all the documentation on all incidents to the Defence and that you now received only the material that you have just provided to us?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This material was with the Defence. I have now taken it. But earlier on I took it from them when I was preparing my expert report.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then, of course, the next question would be to the Defence where the documentation on these incidents -- I don't know whether it's all relevant. I have to check that. But if there is a clear response to that, I'd like to hear it. If it would be not easy at this very moment, I'd prefer that the Defence tries to find it, the reason during the break, and then inform us afterwards. Mr. Ierace -- Mr. Piletta-Zanin, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you for this respite.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: In my respectful submission, it's important to clarify something the witness has said. "I have now taken them from the Defence." Could it be clarified whether this is the same material that he initially received or at least part of the same material he initially received or whether this is a copy of material that he originally received.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We could ask the expert witness to -- to verify that during one of the breaks. Mr. Piletta-Zanin.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I could perhaps answer that, Mr. President. It's impossible to check everything. That's the first matter. And secondly, you know how the work is done. It's quite probable that in such-and-such a series of documents the photocopy of a transcript gets mislaid and then it's then withdrawn and put back into the transcript. So it can't be guaranteed. You can't guarantee the strict authenticity of the documents. But the identity of the documents, yes, this can be guaranteed. But the originality -- the original nature of the documents can't be guaranteed as such because it's possible for documents to be mislaid, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Piletta-Zanin, let's not discuss at this moment what could or not could be done. Let's first try and see what can be done. And then we would afterwards discuss why the results are imperfect, or perhaps perfect. Ms. Pilipovic, we'll hear then an answer on the five incidents after the break. You may proceed in examining the expert witness, Dr. Kunjadic.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Kunjadic, good day. Could you first of all tell us your full name.

utterances.speaker: MILAN KUNJADIC
utterances.text: My name is Milan Kunjadic. My father's name was Ilija. I was born on the 20th of January, 1948 in Drvar. I live and work in Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. When you say that you live and work in Belgrade, can you tell us first of all what your educational background is, which schools you have finished. We have provided your curriculum vitae, but could you briefly tell us which schools you have finished.

utterances.speaker: MILAN KUNJADIC
utterances.text: I finished the Faculty of Science and Mathematics, the section for physical chemistry. Later I finished a specialised course in the police for forensics and also a course for ballistics.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: When you say that you finished a course for criminological technique and for ballistics, can you tell us when this took place and for how long your professional career, so to speak, lasted in the police as a ballistics expert.

utterances.speaker: MILAN KUNJADIC
utterances.text: I worked in the police from 1977 until 1994. I was involved in affairs that had to do with forensic techniques, forensic ballistics. It has to do with the interpretation of material traces caused by firearms. I went through all the training stages. This involved practical work, investigations. I carried out a large number of investigations into firearms.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the witness please approach the microphones.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could you please come closer to the microphone, and Madam Usher will adjust them. Please proceed, Ms. Pilipovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Kunjadic, you say that you carried out a large number of investigations. Can you tell us, first of all, what you're currently involved in.

utterances.speaker: MILAN KUNJADIC
utterances.text: I'm also involved in forensic ballistics. I have an independent agency which is involved exclusively in this sphere. I work at the request of courts. I attend hearings at courts, and I attend the explanation, interpretation of findings at the court.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us, as an expert -- as a ballistics expert, how many cases do you deal with, cases from the sphere of forensic ballistics?

utterances.speaker: MILAN KUNJADIC
utterances.text: That depends on the year. It varies from year to year. But it's between 100 and 150 approximately, annually.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: You told us that you worked at the request of the court, and you said that you also carried out investigations in the police force. Could you briefly tell us the methodology used when carrying out investigation, if we're talking about people who were wounded by firearms.

utterances.speaker: MILAN KUNJADIC
utterances.text: Investigations are carried out on the basis of criminological principles. What is important for my work, it's the criminological technique that is important. It secures and packs and provides material traces. For my expert reports, sketches and photographs of the site are important, and the precise measures of all the traces that are found on the site. These traces identify the trajectory of the projectile and can be used for an expert report which is to be drawn up at a later date and to examine the trajectory of the projectile.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: You've mentioned the methodology. You've told us what is necessary to be done when carrying out an investigation, and you've told us what you, as a forensic ballistics expert, require when investigating people who are wounded by firearms. Can you tell us whether in such situations investigations are always carried out.

utterances.speaker: MILAN KUNJADIC
utterances.text: Investigation is always carried out. All police forces throughout the world do this. They follow universal rules, and it is impossible to draw up an expert report without following such rules. If you fail to carry out an investigation, this can no longer be repeated, and that is why in certain cases, given that certain traces -- the damage caused -- the trace of the damage caused can't be taken, this is why the expert in ballistics is often present when investigations are carried out in order to record and detect the traces and in order to carry out certain measurements on the site which have to be done and perhaps to carry out what we call sighting, if this is necessary, and this means to identify the trajectory through the air, and this is done on the basis of material references, material points that are detected at the site.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Kunjadic, can you therefore tell us what the purpose of the investigation is now that you have told us about this.

utterances.speaker: MILAN KUNJADIC
utterances.text: The purpose is to ensure that the material traces are authentic and to ensure that they have probative value, that is to say, that there are elements that can be used to make a ballistics report later on. So the purpose of investigating is to determine the material traces left by firearms.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: You've told us what the purpose of the investigation is. Can you now tell us who orders an investigation to be carried out and who carries it out.

utterances.speaker: MILAN KUNJADIC
utterances.text: Well, investigative organs order investigations to be carried out. That means the courts in Yugoslavia. And it's usually the organ of interior affairs that carries out the investigation with certain services.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: As a ballistics expert, what is your duty when carrying out an investigation and later on when processing the case?

utterances.speaker: MILAN KUNJADIC
utterances.text: I have told you what the ballistics expert's task is. He has the determine the material traces which are later used for his expert report. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. But criminological technicians are not in a position to understand these traces or to detect these traces. Once these traces at the site have been recorded, then they have to be processed in the ballistics laboratory. First of all, this has to do with the identification of the weapon, of the shell, of the projectile, of the clothes, the point at which the clothes were torn open, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Kunjadic, you tell us that all the traces that are found at the site are analysed. Can you now tell us what can be determined having analysed a projectile or by analysing a projectile which is found at the site?

utterances.speaker: MILAN KUNJADIC
utterances.text: Well, by examining a projectile, it is possible to determine the kind of projectile concerned. It's possible to determine its calibre. It's possible to identify certain deformations either on the side or the front of the projectile. It's also possible to identify the remains of the surface it could have hit if we are talking about a ricochet. It is also possible to identify traces of blood. That would be -- those would be the main things.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Kunjadic, as a ballistics expert, when you receive or have all the necessary elements, can you tell us whether it is possible to determine the distance from which fire was opened, or rather, the distance between the point at which someone was hit from a firearm and the point from which the shot was fired. You as a ballistics expert, when you have all the elements you require, is it possible for you to determine this distance?

utterances.speaker: MILAN KUNJADIC
utterances.text: If you have a sufficient number of elements, it is possible to determine with great precision where the projectile was fired from, with a great degree of precision. It can't be completely precise though. But in addition to these material traces, you'd determine the angle of fall. And on the basis of the calibre of the bullet and ballistics information, one can determine where the shot came from with a great degree of probability, providing that the trajectory -- that in the course of its trajectory, the projectile did not ricochet or if the projectile was not slowed down when penetrating some kind of an obstacle. If we're talking about wounds inflicted on a person, then it is of great importance to carry out a forensic examination, a forensic medical examination of those who died or who were wounded or to carry out a forensic postmortem. Because in terms of ballistics, this is part of the projectile's trajectory, which has to be examined. Since the energy of the projectile is proportional to the penetration of the body, so this can be relevant information for determining the distance from which the projectile was fired.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Kunjadic, can you tell us, to what extent do you as a ballistics expert - and you've told us what you require in order to make a ballistics report - to what extent do you assess -- do you take into consideration the statements of witnesses when you are compiling an expert report?

utterances.speaker: MILAN KUNJADIC
utterances.text: The witness reports are important, and it's one of the main roots of investigation, because in open spaces we wouldn't be able to know from which side a person was hit if this person doesn't tell us that. On the other hand, the problem we have with witness statements concerns the correct interpretation of these statements, and it also has to do with the possibility of determining with precision the position of their body when they were hit because even if -- if the position of the body is not portrayed absolutely correctly, this can have an influence on the determination of the direction of fire. But witness statements are certainly important, but it is not possible to determine these factors only on that basis, if we have no other elements which indicate how the person was wounded.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Kunjadic, after you've answered this question, I'm going to ask you: If a investigation of the scene has not been carried out, the one that you mentioned, either a police of a forensic, later on is it possible to reconstruct and to ascertain the ballistics elements that would be of assistance for a court to decide about the way that a person has been injured, shot from a firearm, or to ascertain the distance from which -- from the firing point in relation to the place where -- location where the person was wounded?

utterances.speaker: MILAN KUNJADIC
utterances.text: The reconstruction of the events have to be followed not only by the witness statement but also the examination of the body by a forensic physician, an expert. In those cases that I have examined, this has not been done in these cases. Now, we do not have the statement of the expert about the identifications of the canals through the body of the injury, of the wound. However, it is possible to do it now if these examinations can be carried out or perhaps if there are x-rays in existence, particularly with projectiles or fragments of projectiles inside a body. Then it will tell a little more about the trajectory of the projectile, and probably we can also tell about the direction where it's come from and the range.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: I'm going to ask you: As a ballistics expert, have you had experience -- and if you have, can you tell us about your experiences about determining the distance from the firing point of a firearm in city surroundings?

utterances.speaker: MILAN KUNJADIC
utterances.text: In most of the cases, it happens in small areas, in closed areas. However, while I was in the police, during celebrations or for New Year's celebrations or sports results, people would fire into the air. And then there would be a large number of projectiles that would then hit apartments, and that's when there were injuries that would take place. On one occasion there was a murder that took place as well. Now, for 12 years -- for 12 New Years, every 1st of January I would examine such incidents, and it was in this sense that I can say that I have experience because I conducted sightings. I carried out the determination of the distance from where -- from where the firearm was shot, the size of the opening or the hole that the projectile left on the window, on the glass, and how shall I put it, we've checked these findings because in many -- on many occasions we carried out identifications. On the other hand, I have also worked in cases in wounding injuries during a hunting, with hunting rifles. That would be all.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: When you've told us that you've had experience in determining the distance, the distance from where the firearm was shot or fired in city surroundings, can you tell us, on the basis of those experiences, is it possible to ascertain the distance in open or in an enclosed space?

utterances.speaker: MILAN KUNJADIC
utterances.text: It's obviously easier in an enclosed space because there are several places that can be pierced through, and it is then easy -- it is possible to establish the distance and that's how you ascertain the distance. And in those cases where you are able to conduct the sighting, the trajectory, then sometimes you can ascertain the exact point, that is, the distance, if distances are not too large.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Now that you've explained the methodology of work, can you tell us the methodology of work in such circumstances - you've told us about the methodology that you use in Yugoslavia so to speak - now, as a ballistics expert, the methodology of work in situations in carrying out investigations and giving your expert opinion, do you know about other countries?

utterances.speaker: MILAN KUNJADIC
utterances.text: Well, victims suffer injury from firearms, whether it's peace or wartime, and the police, they do their work either in peace or in war. So the on-site investigations are carried out in all circumstances. Of course, there are some circumstances when it is not possible for some objective reasons. However, in the incidents that we have processed, usually what was done was the kind of insufficient on-site investigation. So only the operative officer would come out but not the forensic technician or a ballistics expert. And there were probably no reasons for this not to be done. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: I object to that, Mr. President. That's speculative as to what may or may not have happened or why it may or may not have happened.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. That's a comment on the answer of the expert witness. Please proceed, Ms. Pilipovic. And perhaps you could find a suitable moment for a break in up till two or three minutes.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Kunjadic, while you were compiling your written statement that you have submitted to the Chamber, did you have data on the conducted on-site investigations?

utterances.speaker: MILAN KUNJADIC
utterances.text: In my expert report, I listed where the on-site investigations were carried out and where the on-site investigation was carried out, then there was a more successful ascertainment of distance, which I've also explained, in which cases this was so. In all the other cases it was in the beginning when I was explaining about the incident, I would put first of all whether this was done or not, this on-site investigation, so that I would point to the starting points and elements that are necessary for a forensic ballistics analysis, because it is only carried out exclusively, as I've already told you, on the basis of witness statements, on the basis of material traces.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I believe this is a good time for a break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Since we had already 15 minutes off, we'll adjourn until ten minutes past 11.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Ierace.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Just a quick reference to another matter: Mr. Radinovic. The Prosecution is unable to translate the notes that we've been given due to legibility of the witness's handwriting. I respectfully request a typed version of the notes, no amplification, just the words which appear in the notes. And secondly, this, of course, assumes that the Prosecution does not succeed in its recent motion on Mr. Radinovic. The Prosecution seeks from the Defence an indication of the -- that is, the identity of the ABiH orders it proposes to tender, that is, beyond those which are attached to the report by next Wednesday so we can arrange for them to be translated. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Could the Defence indicate what ABiH reports it intends to tender, especially if they've not yet been translated.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think that it is not possible to answer like this straight away. We have to see the documents. We will check and as soon as it's possible, possibly even this afternoon, we'll get in touch with the Prosecution to expand on the document or documents that this is about.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. So I take it that the Defence will, on shortest notice, inform the Prosecution about the documents not referred to in the report but nevertheless intended to be tendered.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And also, Mr. President, you probably have noticed that if it is hard for the Prosecution to read the notes done by the expert, it is also for ourselves. So we have to contact the expert and ask him to do this work. This will take some time, of course. And we will keep you informed or keep the Prosecution informed as much as possible.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Since I do understand that the Defence is willing to seek the cooperation of the expert witness -- Can't you read anything at all? Or is it just then and now a word that you can't read?

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: I'm not sure, Mr. President. I'll have to speak to the language assistant. But --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Because if it's --

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Certainly, it's more than one or two words. I can assure you of that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I do understand. But I don't know how extensive these notes are. I don't know how many words are illegible or not. So before -- and appreciating that the Defence is willing to cooperate, before finally dealing with it, could you please see whether it could be presented in such a way that -- I mean, typing out, especially if it's a lot of text, might take a lot of time. And I don't know whether the expert would have the facilities to do so. But keeping in mind the willingness of the cooperation of the Defence, could we just see how to solve that problem first between the parties before the Chamber gives a final order on it.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Mr. President, I'll make some inquiries or cause some inquiries to be made during the course of today's session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: And update you at the end of the session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: May I ask you, is the -- is the expert witness already -- has he arrived in The Hague, Mr. Piletta-Zanin? No, not --

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, as far as I'm following the schedule that we compiled, Mr. Radinovic will arrive to be heard only after the 20th of February.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I should have consulted my -- the schedule. Let's then at this moment -- Yes, Mr. Ierace.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: He's not due to give evidence until the 3rd and 4th of March.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Let's then -- first of all, that gives more time to prepare for both parties, and so therefore if this would result in a better legible version of the notes, that would certainly be appreciated. And let's now ask the usher to escort Dr. Kunjadic into the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, my co-counsel will continue with the examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Please proceed, Mr. Piletta-Zanin. Please be seated, Dr. Kunjadic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, witness. Can you hear me?

utterances.speaker: MILAN KUNJADIC
utterances.text: Yes, I can. Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Thank you. I'd like to clarify two or three elements of your testimony. I saw that you did not answer a question that you were asked by my colleague, page 33, and this question was about whether you knew how things happened and proceeded in other police forces in the world, in investigations that were necessary. At that time you were interrupted by the Prosecution and you did not continue with your answer. And the question was: What do you know about the techniques used by other police forces elsewhere, apart from the former Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: MILAN KUNJADIC
utterances.text: In the territory of the former Yugoslavia, we all had the same procedure that was followed as far as the police and forensic examinations were concerned. So before the war, we had joint seminars that were held. We held meetings, exchange of opinions, and matters of expert opinions. As far as the forensic technique is concerned and conducting on-site investigations, they were the same. The team is always made up of the operative officer and a crime scene technician, that is, the basic team.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Thank you. Witness, on this subject, you mentioned this need to have experts, that is, specialists, not just technicians, on-site technicians. And you told us that this was the only thing that would allow as a rule to establish scientific conclusion, almost definitive, on the matter in question, that is, the origin and the source of fire. However, what can you tell us as a general rule about hypothetical absence of such researches, examinations, investigations on site.

utterances.speaker: MILAN KUNJADIC
utterances.text: Well, if you don't have anything, if you don't have the basic elements to come to any conclusions, expertly speaking --

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Okay. Well, if I'm going to ask you a more precise question, a more specific question. What is it possible -- how is it possible to do a reconstruction that happens much later, after the fact?

utterances.speaker: MILAN KUNJADIC
utterances.text: It all depends whether it is possible to identify, whether you're able to show the exact spot where the event occurred, whether there are relevant traces on the body, whether it is on the body that you can identify where the bullet has entered the body -- the projectile has entered the body, where it has exited the body, and that would depend on as far as this aspect is concerned. However --

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MILAN KUNJADIC
utterances.text: However, if you do not have this, then the reconstruction will bear no results.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Thank you. You spoke to us about canals, and I think we can imagine what that is -- a channel, correction. And in relation to this channel, what do you mean by that exactly? That is the first question. And is it possible to examine it even under critical circumstances, that is, medical critical circumstances, that is, in time of war? So there are two questions in this one question.

utterances.speaker: MILAN KUNJADIC
utterances.text: In time of war, it all depends on the circumstances, on the possibilities. Probably yes. As far as the channels of the entrance and exit wound, I can only speak about as part of the entire trajectory of the projectile. But this particular aspect is linked to the forensic medical analysis, examination, and it's that expert that is able to give a competent opinion on this.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Thank you. You said - and I'm referring to page 31 - that the position of the body, and that was found on the ground or on another surface, can be determining. In any case, very important. Can you tell us, why is that and how and so on?

utterances.speaker: MILAN KUNJADIC
utterances.text: If you wish to do a reconstruction of events, if there are elements necessary to do this, then you start with the location where the injured person is standing, and this location must be known. That is the starting point of sorts.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: And why is that a starting point?

utterances.speaker: MILAN KUNJADIC
utterances.text: In relation to that point, this is where you can conduct the examination, how was he turned in that moment, what was he doing at that time, and so on. If you don't know the position, you don't know whether he was in a valley, whether he was on a height or an elevated ground, whether he was crouching or standing or in any other position.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Thank you. Witness, I'd like you to listen to my question carefully. Is there a distinction to be made, therefore, between a location of the incident as such and the position of the body after the incident? And if so, what is this distinction?

utterances.speaker: MILAN KUNJADIC
utterances.text: That is also a question that really is for a forensic physician, for a medical expert to give. If a person is hit and if this person was seriously wounded, then he would fall. He would fall next to the place where he was standing. How he fell, that will also be important to see whether there were witnesses or if the person was wounded and then the person himself can tell us about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Thank you. Witness, you spoke to us about what happens in -- at New Year, which happens that sometimes in some parts of the world shots are fired into the air and they cause accidents. That's page 32, line 14. Now, simply, a precision. You said that you investigated several cases of this kind. As a result of your investigations, was it possible to establish whether this was done intentionally [as interpreted]?

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: I object, Mr. President. The question doesn't have any probative value in terms of an event that the witness says happens where he lives, and for that reason it should be withdrawn, in my respectful submission.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, the transcript -- I believe that I was betrayed by the transcript, but I said -- not intentionally, but that's just a detail. May I just respond in the presence of the witness?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. But let's first ask the witness whether your expertise, which as I understand this, ballistic expertise, would allow you to draw any conclusions as to whether wounds caused by firearms have been inflicted intentionally or by error or by mistake. Would your discipline allow you to draw conclusions?

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I asked the witness a question, and I invite him to answer the question.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I never state, and that's not part of my expertise to expand on intentions or lack of intentions. I'm only talking about my expert opinion about trajectory of the projectile and all the other elements.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Piletta-Zanin, let's return to your question.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If I can rephrase. I do not think that I've asked this witness to say whether the result of his examinations would give him the intention. Whether the result of the examination -- the investigation, that is, the police investigation globally, would permit to establish, in terms of looking at forensic ballistics facts, whether it was possible to establish whether this was something that was an accident or done intentionally. That's all. This is just if he knew whether in such-and-such case that he was involved in other services managed to come to the conclusion whether this firing was intentional or unintentional. That's all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, that's now a different question. Whether you are aware of other investigation, not primary ballistics, that could establish whether fire at New Year's eve or -- what festivities was that, Mr. Piletta-Zanin? I have to check that. Yes, that firing in the air at New Year, that the -- whether other investigations would have resulted in an opinion as to whether this was intentionally done or not. Is that -- I have some difficulties in understanding your question precisely, Mr. Piletta-Zanin, because you are talking about shots in the air. Did you expect the victims to be somewhere in the air or ...?

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. Mr. President, it's very simple. It is possible to imagine the Machiavellianism of someone who would use these facts, for instance, to fire intentionally on a third party, commit his crime, hoping that that will be seen as an accident. And the investigation can prove this. It is also possible to establish that shots were fired and they were fired in the air and they unfortunately arrived later and caused victims. So this is a question of stray bullets. So this is what I wanted to find out from the expert in the cases that must be very numerous. What is the reason for these injuries or for these victims, whether this was intentional -- alleged intentional -- I'm sorry, I don't mean to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let me -- I'll put the question to you. Mr. Kunjadic, you said that you were involved in expertise, injuries caused by, may I call it, New Year's firing of firearms. Is there any clue for you whether it's in your expertise or what you heard from others that this fire caused anything else than accidental injuries but, opposed to that, intended injuries?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, I did not take part in such a case. I was not involved in such a case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed, Mr. Piletta-Zanin.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: In these cases that you have mentioned of persons who were hit by bullets during New Year's celebrations, is it possible to find out whether these shots were direct shots or whether these were ricochets? Was this something that you were able to examine?

utterances.speaker: MILAN KUNJADIC
utterances.text: There were cases of both kinds. I don't know individually when and where and what. But in any case, when there is a large number of shots fired, then you have a little bit of everything.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Thank you. Is this something that occurs, these injuries or these deaths, is this something they occur during New Year's celebrations? Is it something that occurred before the war in -- regularly? That is, that every end of the year or one out of two years, according to your experience. How frequent was this?

utterances.speaker: MILAN KUNJADIC
utterances.text: You were not precise.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: I'll rephrase. You told us that you examined several cases of these injuries that happened during New Year's celebrations, end of the year celebrations. These shots, did they happen regularly every year and every year you would have the same problems?

utterances.speaker: MILAN KUNJADIC
utterances.text: Every year there would be firing, but we didn't have injuries every year. I mean, I don't know. We have data from 1994.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, now we'd like to have a look at a tape. But before -- before we do that, in order not to start the machinery rolling, we would like to submit to the witness so that he can recall two maps; the famous incident maps that we by now know by heart. And the one that we're interested in are numbers 11 -- incident number 11 and incident number 3. I would like the witness to have a look at these maps again. He's already had a look at them. He spoke about it earlier. And then we will have a look at tapes in relation to these two specific incidents. I don't know whether we can put these documents on the ELMO, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. But they first have to arrive near to the ELMO.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, we don't have an image.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Neither have we, but -- could the technicians look at it that we receive the ELMO picture on our screen.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Mr. President, in order to save time, I suggest that I continue.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] While we are waiting.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Witness, could you have a look at these two maps -- take these two maps, number 11 and 3, and tell us whether you can recognise them. And could you also tell us whether you were provided with these maps for your expert report, for your technical examination.

utterances.speaker: MILAN KUNJADIC
utterances.text: Yes. These maps were shown to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Very well. Witness, the same question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Since there are extra copies always available for the Bench. And Mr. Ierace, may I take it that you've got a copy as well? So although preferably we work from the ELMO, we'll try to do without and solve the technical problem as soon as possible.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. I don't think it's absolutely necessary. May I continue?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: As soon as the Bench has received their spare copies.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, we have a copy --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar always keeps a few of these maps available. If you would start with 11, Mr. Piletta-Zanin, if that would be possible.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Now?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. That's sufficient.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Witness, would you -- could you take map number 11, please. Do you have it in front of you?

utterances.speaker: MILAN KUNJADIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Thank you. So I have several questions that I would like to put to you. In relation to this type of map, did you or did you not receive for each incident that you analysed maps of this kind? I don't mean identical maps but maps of this kind. Yes or no?

utterances.speaker: MILAN KUNJADIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: We'll now discuss incident number 11. Did you go to the site of the incident?

utterances.speaker: MILAN KUNJADIC
utterances.text: Not to the site of this incident.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Very well. But did you go to other sites?

utterances.speaker: MILAN KUNJADIC
utterances.text: I went to all the sites that I had access to.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Very well. Why didn't you go to this site though?

utterances.speaker: MILAN KUNJADIC
utterances.text: This site hadn't been identified.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Very well. But the area that the map itself shows, did you visit this area? Did you pass through it?

utterances.speaker: MILAN KUNJADIC
utterances.text: Yes, we passed through it.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Very well. Thank you. Witness, what can you tell us about the coordinates on the map in purely geographical terms?

utterances.speaker: MILAN KUNJADIC
utterances.text: Well, you can see that it's an elongated map, that the scale is not the same. It's not correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Could this cause problems for a technician carrying out an investigation? And I'm referring to reading the map.

utterances.speaker: MILAN KUNJADIC
utterances.text: Yes. If you took measurements now, there would be problems because of the scale. You wouldn't get the correct values.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, can we move on to number 3?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, please do so.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Could you take map number 3, please. Have a look at it. And I'd like to ask you the same question about the site. Were you able to gain access to the site?

utterances.speaker: MILAN KUNJADIC
utterances.text: No, I didn't go to this site.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Could you tell us why?

utterances.speaker: MILAN KUNJADIC
utterances.text: Well, this site is in a yard, and when the sites were in flats or in yards, we quite simply did not have the possibility of going there.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Very well. But did you go to a site that was close or sufficiently close to the site?

utterances.speaker: MILAN KUNJADIC
