utterances.text: We passed through the street. We knew that it was the street concerned, but we didn't know where the site was exactly.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Very well. Witness, I would like you to now comment on a cassette. It's cassette number 11 that is going to be shown to us now. Could you watch the cassette carefully, and I will then ask you some questions about it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: There still seems to be no signal on our screens for the video.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Mr. Piletta-Zanin, can you please indicate which videotape you would like played. The video booth has two tapes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It's the one that I provided initially. It should have the number "11" on it. I no longer have the number because the exhibit number is in the booth, but we'll be watching -- we'll see number "11" below. It's incident 11, and that is what we are referring to.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: THE SPEAKER: Mrs. Bajraktarevic, I will now give you some instructions. Please point to the location you were, to the best of your recollection, when Mr. Bosnic was shot. I will now mark an X in yellow paint on the pavement. And beside the X, I marked a small arrow pointing to the top of the wall. Please point to the best of your recollection to the location where Mr. Bosnic was gathering wood when you heard the shot.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. They have to stop -- they have to stop the video. The tape is about a protected --

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Mr. President. It's what I wanted to verify. It's what I was verifying with my colleague. And I suggest that we should go into private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We'll first go into closed session.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Witness, with regard to this cassette, the type of information provided by this person in response to the questions that the investigator put to her, in your opinion, is this information sufficient to determine something in terms of ballistics?

utterances.speaker: MILAN KUNJADIC
utterances.text: The witness didn't precisely indicate the position of the injured party. She only pointed to an area which she didn't define precisely. She just pointed in the direction of that area. So even if we wanted to reconstruct the event, it wouldn't be possible for us to place the injured party in the position where he was, not even approximately. So the information required for a ballistics expert report is lacking.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Thank you. Are there any other technical observations that you could make about the procedure such as it was demonstrated in the video?

utterances.speaker: MILAN KUNJADIC
utterances.text: Well, I don't know what you are referring to. All you can see is that the site has been covered by vegetation. Whether it was the case when the incident occurred itself, I don't know. So although an investigation team went there, we don't have any information on the exact look, appearance of the site, or the position where the injured party was when the projectile was fired.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Thank you. I'll go back to what you said a minute ago. Before the break, you spoke about variations in the trajectory in a closed space, I think that's the term we used, because a projectile could have left traces, it could deviate, it could be hindered in the course of its trajectory, it could encounter obstacles. Do you remember talking about this?

utterances.speaker: MILAN KUNJADIC
utterances.text: Yes. What is missing here is a forensic medical --

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: I'll stop you there. You mentioned vegetation. Is it possible that in open spaces, in rural areas, is it possible that the projectile is deviated from its course because it passes through leaves, through vegetation, branches, et cetera?

utterances.speaker: MILAN KUNJADIC
utterances.text: The projectile can deviate in the sense that it is subject to ricochet. But this can't be caused by soft material, leaves and so on. This can be caused by hard material, stones, wood, for example. But grass and leaves can't present such an obstacle.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Thank you. Before we prepare cassette number 3, which is the following one, which we will view in closed session if possible, could you tell us on the basis of your personal experience what the situation is with regard to what we call stray bullets. As an expert, is this a phenomenon that can occur frequently in wartime conditions?

utterances.speaker: MILAN KUNJADIC
utterances.text: Well, I really couldn't say whether this occurs frequently or not. There are such projectiles. So I can't answer that with precision. Usually one is referring to projectiles which ricochet, which change their trajectory, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Thank you. If we have a wounded person at a given site but in an area where fighting is ongoing, is there a possibility of scientifically and technically excluding the possibility of a stray bullet? Can this possibility be excluded?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Before the witness answers this question, I'd like to -- him to define what a stray bullet exactly is. You said, "Usually one is referring to projectiles which ricochet, which change their trajectory, et cetera." Would you, before answering a question, the question by Mr. Piletta-Zanin, give a clear definition of when you consider a bullet to be a stray bullet.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] When, for example, the bullet misses its target and hits a target that it wasn't supposed to hit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And how from a ballistics point of view would you know whether the object that was hit by the bullet was intended by the person who fired, and is there a ballistic way of establishing whether the bullet hit the intended target or any other object?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. I was thinking of areas which aren't visible. For example, if there is a man in the grass. If the man is not visible but is hit by a bullet. So this is what I was thinking of, of the area itself where such things happen. But from a ballistics point of view, it's impossible for me to know whether the shot was fired intentionally or not. Naturally, I'm not talking about these things.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. My next question: You said about an area where you could not see the person. Let's just assume for argument's sake that one would expect someone to be in the grass although not visible but the grass is visible, would you then if such a person -- although invisible from where the person firing was located, would you consider this a stray bullet or ...?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I haven't fully understood your question. If the person is hidden in the grass --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I understood that you gave an example of where you would accept a bullet is a stray bullet when it hit a person or an object that could not be seen from the location where the person firing was positioned. And then this example was about a person hit by a bullet hidden in the grass. And my question to you was whether if one would have a suspicion that someone would have been in the grass, although not visible, if such a person would have been hit while being in the grass, whether you would consider this to be a stray bullet or not.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. If the person -- if a person is hidden in the grass, and I'm aware of the fact that naturally the bullet is not a stray one.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Therefore, from a ballistics point of view, you could not identify a bullet to be a stray bullet but you could describe circumstances which would make it more or less probable. Is that a correct understanding of what your expertise could tell us?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Would you please keep in mind this, Mr. Piletta-Zanin, when putting the next questions to the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Indeed, Mr. President. But I believe that as far as this aspect is concerned, the witness has replied, has answered. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Witness, could you please focus on the tape that we will now show in a minute.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] But, Mr. President, we have to say, as Madam Registrar is just doing -- we have to go into closed session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We'll turn into closed session.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Witness, I want to ask you certain questions, and I'll be very grateful that if we are speaking about the person that we just saw on this videotape, the person who was injured, can you please never mention the name. Just speaking of her as "the person" or "the victim." Thank you. On this subject, what can you tell us in relation to the ballistics technique of the positions that were marked on the wall by the investigator, particularly in relation to the first step and in relation to the position of the person in question, the way that she's described it herself on the first step.

utterances.speaker: MILAN KUNJADIC
utterances.text: Here we have -- how shall I put it? -- A partial reconstruction, so to speak, of the position of the body of the injured party. But as I've spoken of this earlier, what's insufficient here is that we do not Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. have the direction of the channels of the -- inside her body, the part of the back where she was wounded. What I'm saying is that as we can see on the videotape, she showed the position that she had, which was a crouching position. And if the projectile was going down her back, because it was supposed to injure her, then on one side it must have come from a height but then it couldn't have hit the wall on the other side. If the person was crouching with her body differently, then the direction of the firing would have been almost parallel to the ground. Now, between the first mark point where the bullet hit and the height of where her feet were, the way it's assessed, the way we can assess from the videotape without measuring anything - although, this should have been done, the measurements - is about 30 centimetres. Which means that if the position of the person in a crouching position, leaning forward, that should be -- should have been- again, I'm assessing because it's insufficient because of the medical documentation - then what should have been done, that it should have been above the spot where the projectile had hit. The projectile must have come somewhere from the front side. Of course, we don't know exactly from where and from which side because what should have been done is that forensically it should have been processed by the crime technician on the site the impact spot of the projectile, then to establish the position, which cannot always be established but at least then what can be supposed where the direction where the shot was fired from. There is another possibility in this incident, which is that the projectile hit -- had hit the wall, that it fragmented and that it -- fragments of the fragmented projectile, that is, fragments of the jacket, the jacket of the bullet, would have hit or had injured her. But that is a supposition on the basis of which I cannot draw any certain conclusions. That is the reason why there is basis and reasons to ask for a reconstruction, while this reconstruction, it's supposed to be done, it should be done with the person who was of -- who is of similar physical characteristics as the injured party at the time when she was injured.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, counsel. Microphone, counsel. Microphone, counsel. Microphone, counsel.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Microphone.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Witness, you spoke to us of a jacket, of a bullet, of a projectile. Now, my question is the following: In practice, if a projectile explodes or fragments, disintegrates on a hard surface, these fragments, can they still travel in space? And if so, what is the distance that they can travel to? That is, is this something that is very -- do they go very near the impact position or can they go a lot further away than that? What can you tell us about it?

utterances.speaker: MILAN KUNJADIC
utterances.text: The projectile fragments, disintegrates, and in this case we do not know what kind of a projectile that was and what kind of energy it would have had, generated. But it certainly should have had a higher energy in order to decompose fragments, depending on the weapon that's fired. Because what happens with a projectile is that it loses its force on impact and then the fragments cannot go very far.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Witness, my questions were more of a general nature. According to your knowledge in the area of ballistics, and assuming that a bullet or a projectile fragments -- disintegrates on impact, is it possible theoretically speaking that these fragments continue to travel along distance and can injure several people? Is this something that's envisageable? Is it possible, on a basis of principle, as a general rule, is this possible?

utterances.speaker: MILAN KUNJADIC
utterances.text: Disintegrated fragments on short distances have the energy that at short distances - and I mean from the impact point where the projectile hit, so several metres - the fragment can injure the person, it can hit the person. If the angle of the firing into the hard surface is such that there was a partial decomposition, fragmentation of the projectile, that it ricochetted, then that fragment which remains then at certain distances, if it's a large fragment, it can cause injury.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Thank you. Witness, I'm going to come back to the case that we just saw. You spoke to us, if I understood you correctly, of a necessity of an elevated angle depending on whether the person who was fired at -- the way the person was fired at? Did I understand you correctly?

utterances.speaker: MILAN KUNJADIC
utterances.text: What I said is that on the video, we saw a crouching position. While, I don't know whether the projectile went under the skin from up -- from up to down or in another way. If it went from up to down under the skin onto the back, then that position would be -- wouldn't correspond to certain distances.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Very well. Now, once -- when you were establishing your report, the person that you saw, was this person younger -- was this person smaller because she was younger at the time? This is something that you knew. You did take that into consideration.

utterances.speaker: MILAN KUNJADIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes. Yes, I did. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: No, I withdraw that.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Would you allow me one additional question in respect for my better understanding.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Previous interpretation continues] ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: When you say that you saw a crouching person, is it your interpretation of the video that the person as it was positioned when asked to take the position was exactly there or somewhere else? Because in one of the earlier questions, the investigator asks her, I think, to tell where her feet or her legs were on a step. Did you interpret the position taken by the crouching person to be the actual position where she was hit or just to demonstrate what her body position if not exactly on that place would have been? Could you tell us how you interpreted that in order to better understand your conclusions.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just in relation to the position, the way she was crouching. Not in relation to the position on site, on the scene.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I'm just trying to understand whether I understood you well. You say the body position she demonstrated, you did not interpret that to be at the exact spot where she was hit. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's correct. Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Please proceed, Mr. Piletta-Zanin.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Mr. President, I'd like us to move on to another incident, which is incident number 13. And I know that we will manage to produce miracles in producing maps. But I do not know whether the video -- rather, the ELMO is working now. Very well. In which case -- thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Witness, the same question: Do you recognise this map? Was this something that you saw? Was it submitted to you?

utterances.speaker: MILAN KUNJADIC
utterances.text: Yes, it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Thank you. Witness, could you please be given a pointer. Thank you. Witness, on this map, could you please indicate so that we can make sure, could you indicate the building known as the UN building today. At the time that was a student hostel.

utterances.speaker: MILAN KUNJADIC
utterances.text: [Indicates]

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Could you point at the second of those buildings.

utterances.speaker: MILAN KUNJADIC
utterances.text: [Indicates]

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Very well. Yes. Thank you. So you've identified for the transcript the two buildings -- the two student hostels. And were you in that area? Did you go to that area?

utterances.speaker: MILAN KUNJADIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Thank you. Witness, can you point to the road which is located there marked in red to the south of the buildings, the student hostels, that is, linking Nedzarici area and the Alipasino Polje, that is, Vojnicko Polje -- no, no. Perpendicular, which goes -- can you see a road to the south of the building which is the student building, not south-east. I meant south. Go higher, higher, higher. Stop. No, just go down.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Piletta-Zanin, are you inviting the witness to point at the road that goes from point 13 into a circle a bit south-east -- south-west of that?

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's perfect, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. From point 13, just south-east, that road. Would you point at it.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Indicates]

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Here it is. Thank you. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Now, witness, when you were doing your analysis, were you informed of the existence of barricades at the time of these events which was located somewhere in that portion of the road? And if so, how much were you told?

utterances.speaker: MILAN KUNJADIC
utterances.text: Yes, I did know that barricades had been erected because I was there at the time of these demonstrations when the investigator had been doing this case in Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: No, witness. What I'm trying to say, that barricades that were erected - and we mean barricades, for instance, containers that were erected as protection so that shots cannot hit those that are behind those barricades. Sometimes they're called as fronts or barricades.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Ierace.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Mr. President, I object to leading on this particular issue.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. The objection is sustained. Could you tell us anything about any artificial obstructions that you would under normal circumstances not find in that area, specifically on that road? Were you informed about it? And what could you tell us what your information was?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Looking at this case, studying this case, I bore it into mind at the time in Sarajevo I was -- when the investigator was doing this incident. And the exact point on the crossroad was shown where the barricades had been positioned. So I do know about this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Now, what kind of barricades were these? What was it made of, as far as you were informed?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I can't recall right now what the barricades were.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could you indicate where you did -- where they were positioned on this map?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] They were positioned at crossroads itself or next to the intersection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Were you aware of any other obstructions - and by "obstructions" I mean in whatever way preventing the use of roads for what they are for, that is, to pass through - are you aware of the existence of any other obstructions? Did you receive any information --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, no. As far as other information is concerned, at the time when I was doing the expert report, I don't know whether there were other barricades or not -- other obstacles or not.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Obstacles. No obstacles that would take either access or view, apart from those already mentioned? If you don't know, just tell us. I'm not trying to ...

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't know about any others. I've already answered the question, I believe.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you. Please proceed, Mr. Piletta-Zanin.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Mr. President. Thank you for rephrasing all of this.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: My question, in fact, was the following: Witness, you had your findings and your report on incident number 13. I'm going to ask you a hypothetical question. If on the road that you mentioned earlier there had been several other obstacles, would that have changed your opinion? What can you tell us about that? If there had been several other barricades, for instance. It is a hypothetical question, I know, but still.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Piletta-Zanin, even then, if you are asking whether it would change the opinion of the expert, would you not first see what his opinion was so then we can then identify what might or might not have changed.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Absolutely.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Absolutely.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: So, witness, can you please tell us, what was the result, the findings of your examination for incident number 13?

utterances.speaker: MILAN KUNJADIC
utterances.text: Well, I said that the projectile that had hit - and that's obvious - it fragmented. We do not have a defined channel, which channel on the vehicle or where it could indicate where this was fired from. According to the documents, it was fired from the right-hand side of the vehicle which was going up and from those defragmented projectiles -- projectile, that is, the fragments, persons were injured. So what can certainly be established, according to the description, is from which side of the vehicle the projectile came. But the exact direction and all other elements that could get us closer to defining the position, it is not possible to ascertain that. There are simply not enough elements.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Witness, I'm going to ask you to recall as much as you can. You told us about a relative velocity and the space theoretical of the shot. Now, if we are talking about a theoretical speed of a vehicle and the speed or the velocity of a projectile in the case of this incident, what can you give us as a general indication?

utterances.speaker: MILAN KUNJADIC
utterances.text: Well, it is possible to say something about it. If you have --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the witness repeat the beginning of the answer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could you please repeat the beginning of your answer, because the interpreters couldn't catch it.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So again, it is in connection, in relation to the lack of -- shortage of elements. Because what has not been given is what the speed of the vehicle was, which is important. If the vehicle was moving at 40 kilometres an hour - and this is just a supposition - then it's going 90 metres a second. Now, if it's going 60 kilometres an hour, then it's going about 15 metres a second. So in relation to this, depending on how far the shot has come from, from which distance, and whether the vehicle is being targeted, whether we wish to hit it on the spot which we can see on the video recording that was presented by the Prosecution and that the investigator on the scene of the incident marked with paint, the distance from the barricade to the scene where the shooting occurred is very short. If we want to hit a vehicle which is moving at the speed of, for instance, 40 kilometres an hour, then you have to -- you have to take that into consideration where it's going to be. It's like hunting. When a bird is flying, so you have to take the distance into consideration, the distance it will travel by the time the bullet gets there. So that the vehicle and the projectile will come and reach the same point. So in this case, perhaps it was by a length it was just behind the barricade. So this is all theoretical. This is all a supposition. Then it should have just covered that distance within a very short period of time. So whether you waited for that vehicle to emerge, again, depending on the distance, but perhaps 400, 500 metres, you would have to miss it. Because if it was 500 metres in one second, the bullet covers that distance - or less than a second - the vehicle is already gone. So there are many unknown factors, unknown elements - and this is just an example - which could point to that, that the vehicle was perhaps hit by a projectile that could have been fired a little bit earlier than the vehicle was actually spotted. It's again a -- an assumption or a supposition because we don't know whether the vehicle was actually spotted. The moment when it just emerged behind the barricade or just before or just after. So in this case, I am not ascertaining -- saying anything. I am just explaining the problems -- elaborating on the problems of identifying the position from where -- from where the shot is fired, that is, the establishing of the position, of that position. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Can the speeds and distances covered per second be clarified with the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I had some difficulties also where the witness said that 40 kilometres an hour would result in 90 metres a second, I think. But perhaps it's a translation problem. In the very beginning of your answer you said something about the speed of the vehicle. You linked --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 9 or 10. 9 or 10 metres in a second.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: 9 or 10 metres in a second, yes. And then for 60, you said it would be 15 approximately.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Roughly speaking. Yes. There is information -- there is data on this. It's possible to calculate it.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Thank you. Witness, in your testimony you spoke about what we call a window, a firing window, the place where it's possible for a shot to be fired. And my question is as follows: Your conclusions with regard to incident number 13, would they have been different or would you have supported these conclusions if you were told that there was not just one barrier, not just one obstacle, but several obstacles along the road that you mentioned a minute ago?

utterances.speaker: MILAN KUNJADIC
utterances.text: I said that we don't know exactly where the projectile was fired from, but if there's someone behind an obstacle, then this obstacle will obviously cause a problem. An obstacle is an obstacle. Whether it's an adequate one or not, I simply don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, could we show the map for incident 2, and then I'll show video that concerns incident number 2.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Piletta-Zanin, if you turn to another incident, and in order to prevent that we have to get back to the problem. I'd like to seek a clarification from the witness. When you were asked about the speed of the vehicle and of the speed in also metres per second, did you tell us this because of the time the bullet would need to travel - that's just for sake of argument assumed - the time the bullet would take to travel from the circle indicated on the map to the place that was shown to you as the place of impact and the time the vehicle would need to -- to pass the crossroad? Is that what you're drawing our attention to?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That was an example, and that's what I wanted to draw your attention to.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: May I then ask you: Since you've visited the site, at what length the road can be observed from what was indicated to you as a possible source of fire, which was as I did understand you well at approximately 500 metres? What -- at what length the intersection could be observed from that position? Would that have been 10 metres, 20 metres, 30 metres, or didn't you measure it, or don't you have an impression of --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I didn't measure that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Did I understand you well that in order to hit from the assumed source of fire, that in order not to make it a lucky shot that you would need first time for pulling the trigger once you see that vehicle and that then there would be time needed for the bullet to travel at such a distance and that one should take into consideration how -- at what length at this intersection the vehicle could be seen? Is that a correct understanding of your testimony?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, you've understood my testimony correctly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Please then proceed, Mr. -- We have to look at the clock. How much time would the Defence still need, Mr. Piletta-Zanin?

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Not much time, Mr. President, but I'll confer with my colleague. How much time do we have left, if I may ask?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, I think that I have no clear instruction to be given, since this type of expert -- expertise, it's not always easy to give an assessment of what would be needed for a clear explanation of the expertise. That's perhaps a bit different to the background. But of course, I -- I must say that the report as such is very clear, and it certainly was of use to have some additional observations. But if you try to make it as efficient as possible. And you say you would not need much time. But could you give us an indication? Would it be ten minutes, a quarter of an hour?

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, what we suggest is the following: We should watch one more incident on a video to see what a technical expert thinks about how the technical aspect was presented by the Prosecution, and then we would like the witness to confirm his report, since he is here under oath, and then I have some general questions I would like to put. But we won't examine each element individually. There is incident 2 that I want to examine. And during the break, I can provide the technical booth with the material required. At what time will we be having a break?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then I suggest that we would have a break now, because then there would be only 40 minutes left after the break. So I take it then you'll take one more video, ask the witness about the collection of data as shown on that video. You'll not go through each and every incident, which is understandable, because most of the conclusions were in the negative and then you have a few additional questions. Could I just suggest to you that all together 20 minutes would do for that?

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Yes. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then we'll adjourn until five minutes past 1.00, and then you have time until five -- 25 minutes past 1.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed, Mr. Piletta-Zanin. I take it that the video is ready?

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Willingly. But perhaps it will be useful for the expert to be present. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: For that time, if I could take advantage of these few seconds. The language assistants can only interpret the names and dates. We have put in an urgent request to CLSS to advise us whether they think they can do any better. We should know that by late this afternoon. I will, therefore, inform you on Monday. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then I do agree with you, Mr. Piletta-Zanin, that for reasons of transparency, it's good that the expert witness testifying is present in the court. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I'll be as clear as possible. But in order to avoid any confusion with regard to the cassette, we believe that there are no problems. But perhaps it would be better to view it in closed session. That won't bother us.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: There are no protective measures --

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, as far as we know, there aren't any protective measures.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We can play it in open session. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Could you show the cassette, please. And at the same time, could we place the map on the ELMO.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That was a bit too fast for me. Could we view it again at a normal speed.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: THE SPEAKER: Could you please show me by pointing where to the best of your recollection you heard gunfire shortly before your daughter Anisa was shot. Thank you. Could you now please show me where to the best of your recollection the bullet hole was before the wall was repaired. I can see traces of repair work on the wall at this location, and I am going to place small red marks with a red tip felt pen.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Witness, could you comment on the methodology and on this type of incident.

utterances.speaker: MILAN KUNJADIC
utterances.text: I briefly explained in the expert report that an investigation wasn't carried out, that the traces weren't established, that the angle of incidence of the projectile is not known. And likewise, whether it was a direct hit or not is another factor that remains unknown. Statements can be examined, of course, but the most essential thing is to determine how the person was wounded, in what position the person was when that person was wounded in the right leg in relation to the origin of the projectile. If the person was towards the house, then the right leg should have been towards the wall. If he was coming out of the house, then the person should have been facing the place from which the projectile apparently arrived. And therefore, my opinion is the same as in the case of incident number 3. It's necessary to carry out a forensic examination of the channel of the wound because there is a possibility, and this is always the case with a projectile that disintegrates, it's possible for wounds to be caused by fragments of the projectile. In this case, we don't have any information as to whether the projectile went across the leg, through the leg, or whether it hit the leg lengthwise, and this would be necessary to determine what the position of the body was. Everything remains within the domain of statements. Everything is reduced to statements. And this has to be verified from the point of view of forensics. It has to be checked to see whether this is the case.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Witness, thank you. I have the following questions: You spoke about a direct shot. Am I to deduce that according to your examination in this specific case, one can't say that yes, in fact it does concern a direct hit or it's an indirect shot, in fact, it's a ricochet or the result of fragments or something like that?

utterances.speaker: MILAN KUNJADIC
utterances.text: Well, I have just explained why it was impossible for me to state an opinion.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Very well. I wanted to make sure that I had understood you. What you have told us about the technical impossibility to say whether this concerned a direct shot or not is this something that you encountered in the course of your investigations in relation to several of the case examined? Did you encounter the same difficulty?

utterances.speaker: MILAN KUNJADIC
utterances.text: Well, the forensic medical expert determines whether it was a direct hit or not, and it's on the basis of the entry wound or the entry and exit wound, on this basis, that the character of the wound is determined. Whether it's a circular or an elliptical wound, the expert determines whether there are any -- whether any irregular damage has been caused. The expert also determines the nature of the channels of the wound, and these factors are taken into consideration when deciding whether it's a direct hit or not. When I say "a direct hit," that means that the projectile entered or penetrated the body in a regular manner.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Very well. If I have understood you correctly, this is in the technical domain. And when you speak about the channel, the result of a ricochet could also cause direct entry to a certain extent, could also result in direct entry.

utterances.speaker: MILAN KUNJADIC
utterances.text: There are probably such cases, but it's difficult to distinguish them because especially in cases when there's a slight deviation or rebound from a soft surface, the deformation of the projectile will not be very great and the projectile will hit the body in a regular manner and make a so-called circular wound, and this will appear as if the shot -- it will appear as if the shot were direct.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Thank you. Witness, the second question that I would like to ask you with regard to the video has to do with the fact that the witness who was interrogated was asked to say where in his opinion the shot came from on the basis of what he had heard. My question is as follows: If we are in an urban area, is it possible for one to hear where the shot came from? Is it possible to determine the origin of the shot on the basis of what one hears?

utterances.speaker: MILAN KUNJADIC
utterances.text: Well, we've all heard shots or explosions in urban areas. We know that sound rebounds from walls, that there is a fact of reverberation. It's difficult to locate the origin of sound. Perhaps if someone gets accustomed to these things or knows in advance where the shot will be fired from, but I don't have any particular opinion about this.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Well, this question no longer has anything to do with this video, but it's of a general kind. In wartime, when there are several positions from which fire can be opened, in your opinion does this increase the difficulty of determining the origin of the fire on the basis of what is heard?

utterances.speaker: MILAN KUNJADIC
utterances.text: Well, yes, of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Thank you. Witness, another question, and I think we will have finished. As a matter of principle, can you -- could you formally confirm before this Trial Chamber -- could you formally confirm the conclusions that you reached in your expert report?

utterances.speaker: MILAN KUNJADIC
utterances.text: Well, yes, I do confirm the conclusions I reached in my expert report.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise. I -- thank you. Mr. President, I would just like to confer with my colleague for 15 seconds, with your leave. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Please do so.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: My last question: You mentioned on several occasions in the report that you have just confirmed the lack of basic documents or other elements of evidence. I'm not just referring to bullets but all the elements in technical reports that are required according to you. My question is as follows: Can you explain why this was the case? That's my first question.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: I object, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Well, given the answer, which is unsurprising, I withdraw my objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Previous interpretation continues] ...

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Do you know -- I'll rephrase that. Do you know whether there is a general obligation for the authorities, for the police, to preserve the projectiles in the course of an investigation, in case an investigation -- if an investigation is carried out?

utterances.speaker: MILAN KUNJADIC
utterances.text: In Belgrade, yes, they're kept for a long period of time.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No further questions, Mr. President, unless my colleague is suddenly inspired.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Previous interpretation continues] ... Put to the expert witness, she is invited to put -- to do so.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Kunjadic, you told us that as a professional man, a ballistics expert, you said that in order to make your report it was necessary for you to have a record of the investigation. And from your expert report this is possible to conclude, so to speak, that you mentioned as one of the reasons the lack of the record of the investigation. You couldn't use them because you didn't have them. If these investigations weren't carried out, can you tell us what the reason is for this?

utterances.speaker: MILAN KUNJADIC
utterances.text: I really don't know. I can assume --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Previous interpretation continues] ... This question has been asked by Mr. Piletta-Zanin. It was objected against by Mr. Ierace. The witness quite understandably responded already that he wouldn't know because I take it that you were not present when all the --

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Perhaps I wasn't following carefully.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Ierace, is the Prosecution ready to start cross-examination of the expert witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Yes, thank you, Mr. President. Perhaps the -- perhaps the ELMO might be moved slightly so that I can see the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Madam Usher, could you please re-establish eye contact between Prosecution and expert witness. You'll now be examined, Dr. Kunjadic, by counsel for the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. Kunjadic. Could you tell us, sir, when it was, perhaps what month, what year, that you received from the Defence the statements and police reports and maps that you mention in your report.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Do you recall what month?

utterances.speaker: MILAN KUNJADIC
utterances.text: No, I do not.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: And whereabouts today are those documents?

utterances.speaker: MILAN KUNJADIC
utterances.text: All documents are with the Defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: When did you give them back to the Defence?

utterances.speaker: MILAN KUNJADIC
utterances.text: After the first expanded version was completed, I don't recall.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Well, what year was that?

utterances.speaker: MILAN KUNJADIC
utterances.text: Probably in 2001.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: All right. As you understood it, did you do that report before the trial had commenced or not?

utterances.speaker: MILAN KUNJADIC
utterances.text: The first version, the expanded version of the report, I compiled it before the trial. And then we waited for the trial. And what I wished to do was also to hear the testimony of Witness Hinchliffe, and that's why we didn't give the final version.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Did you return the material to the Defence towards the end of 2001?

utterances.speaker: MILAN KUNJADIC
utterances.text: I said I really don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MILAN KUNJADIC
utterances.text: Probably, but I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: When was the next time you received any material from the Defence?

utterances.speaker: MILAN KUNJADIC
utterances.text: I received -- I was given the task that the transcript from the trial should be translated so that I can see what this is about, because I -- my English isn't very good, so the Defence engaged a translator who worked with me reading through the transcript and establishing the differences between the previously given statements and those statements that were given in testimony and trial.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Yes. You told us this morning that was last summer. And you said, "Because I understood that there were no considerable differences, I then didn't quote them in any special way," them being the transcript. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MILAN KUNJADIC
utterances.text: That's right. I didn't quote them. I didn't list them in the report. I didn't quote anything from the transcripts.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Did you understand that you were given the transcript of all of the evidence given by the witnesses that were relevant to the sniping incidents?

utterances.speaker: MILAN KUNJADIC
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: I suppose it took a long time for that to be -- I withdraw that. I suppose it took a long time for that to be read through.

utterances.speaker: MILAN KUNJADIC
utterances.text: Yes. The transcript is very long, yes, and we needed a lot of time.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: All right. And then I take it it was after that exercise of going through the transcript that you completed your report. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MILAN KUNJADIC
utterances.text: That's correct. I redrafted the first expanded version of the report I had because it was far too long and I was advised to cut it short, which I did, and that was the final version of my report.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: And you did that redrafting after you had become familiar with the evidence given in court; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MILAN KUNJADIC
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: And was your report completed in October 2002?

utterances.speaker: MILAN KUNJADIC
utterances.text: Yes, in October 2002. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Were you given any directions from the Defence in terms of using material that had not been admitted into evidence in the trial?

utterances.speaker: MILAN KUNJADIC
utterances.text: Yes, I have. Yes. I was given directions.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: What were you told?

utterances.speaker: MILAN KUNJADIC
utterances.text: I was told that the relevant statements are those that were witness statements of the witnesses who came to testify.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: And were you given the same directions in relation to documents that you relied upon, such as police reports, whether you should only rely on documents if they had been tendered into evidence?

utterances.speaker: MILAN KUNJADIC
utterances.text: No. I was given instructions not to rely on police documents, statements that were given to the police. At the police, that is -- they were not relevant.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Why, then, did you mention police documents in your assessment of some incidents?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: May I just interfere at this very moment. Could I please -- You answered the question about police reports. Your answer: "I was given instructions not to rely on police documents, statements that were given to the police." Your answer relates to a slightly different category, I would say, as the question. The question was about police reports, and your answer was about, as I understood it to be, witness statements given to the police. Could you please specify your answer, whether you were instructed not to use police reports - that means reports drawn by the police, not limited to what witnesses would have told them - and statements, that is, written-down wording or at least summaries of what witnesses had told the police.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As far as police reports are concerned, it was said that those were relevant that are in relation to the on-site investigations and that the others were not relevant.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: All right. So when you said that you were instructed not to rely on police reports, you intended to limit your answer to the reports of witness statements and not -- that you were not instructed not to use the police reports dealing with the investigations by the police itself on the spot?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, for me it is a little difficult to understand your question. What I said was that I was using the reports, that is, sketches, photo file, from the site. And whatever has been done on site by the forensic and technical part. But any other parts of that that should not be used, then I didn't use them. That's how I do my work even now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. It clarifies sufficiently. Mr. Ierace, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Approximately how long did it take you to go through the -- the transcript of the evidence? Was it a matter of hours or days or weeks?

utterances.speaker: MILAN KUNJADIC
utterances.text: Days. I came on several occasions. I would stay, and we would compare the transcripts and the previously given statements. It was voluminous material, and it went -- proceeded very slowly.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: When you say "we would compare," you and who else?

utterances.speaker: MILAN KUNJADIC
utterances.text: The translator. The translator who was translating the transcript for me and myself.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Do you have a copy of your report in front of you?

utterances.speaker: MILAN KUNJADIC
utterances.text: Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: I think there is a subheading very early on in the report, immediately after the contents, titled "Request for expertise." Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: MILAN KUNJADIC
utterances.text: [No audible response]

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: In that section, do you set out the various materials that were provided to you in order for you to prepare your report?

utterances.speaker: MILAN KUNJADIC
utterances.text: On page 2, do you say?

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Under heading "1. Request for expertise."

utterances.speaker: MILAN KUNJADIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Do you have a B/C/S or English version that you're reading? That's in Serbian, is it, the one you --

utterances.speaker: MILAN KUNJADIC
utterances.text: In B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MILAN KUNJADIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: All right. Now, in that section, do you mention anything at all about your consideration of the evidence given in court?

utterances.speaker: MILAN KUNJADIC
utterances.text: No, not here. I don't speak here of testimony. That part remained from the previous version of the report. As I've explained, the -- those documents were compared, and I did not mention the witness testimony in court.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Did you mention the fact that you consulted the testimony in court, did you mention that fact anywhere at all in this report?

utterances.speaker: MILAN KUNJADIC
utterances.text: No, I didn't mention it. I explained that I was comparing them. I didn't find these elements.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Looking back on it, was it not appropriate to inform those who read the report that you had consulted the evidence given in court?

utterances.speaker: MILAN KUNJADIC
utterances.text: I can say that the way that I work and the way I work in Belgrade is that all the statements -- but I'm not -- I take them out of the evidence with all the relevant elements. But as I was told to cut short my version, I then shortened it and I used the sentence that I was using everything from the documents, and I meant these data, these relevant documents that were at my disposal.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Would you please answer the question. On reflection, do you not think it was appropriate to include in your report the fact that you had consulted the evidence given in court?

utterances.speaker: MILAN KUNJADIC
utterances.text: Now I can see that. Yes, absolutely.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: All right. Would you please turn to incident number 17. Do you have that page in front of you?

utterances.speaker: MILAN KUNJADIC
utterances.text: Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Do you agree with me that what appears under the heading "Incident no. 17" is confirmed to a consideration of the statement of Fatima Osmanovic? In other words, the source of information was the statement of Fatima Osmanovic.

utterances.speaker: MILAN KUNJADIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Did she give evidence?

utterances.speaker: MILAN KUNJADIC
utterances.text: Whether she testified I cannot recall. It is possible -- just a moment. No, she did not testify.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: What are you now consulting? What is the piece of paper that you just consulted?

utterances.speaker: MILAN KUNJADIC
utterances.text: It's a piece of paper with the witnesses, witness testimonies. They're all -- rather, the witnesses who came to testify during the trial.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: All right. Might I have access to that. And whilst I'm having access, can you tell me this: When you spent those days going through the transcript, how could it possibly be that in relation to incident number 17, you did not realise that Fatima Osmanovic did not even give evidence?

utterances.speaker: MILAN KUNJADIC
utterances.text: I looked at her as an injured party that had injuries and that these injuries were obvious from --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: One moment. One moment, please. Madam Usher, could you please -- Mr. Ierace, could you please return it to Madam Usher since just before handing it out Mr. Piletta-Zanin -- Yes. No. I'm not saying that you -- I would like to give an opportunity to Mr. Piletta-Zanin since he was standing. No, no, no, no, no. Was there anything you would like to say, Mr. Piletta-Zanin? Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, counsel, please. Microphone. Microphone.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Microphone.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Mr. President. It is useless for me to see the document. But why I am objecting and what I really do not appreciate it is the tone. On several occasions you have told the parties that the answers can be achieved if the tone is adequate. Now, if the witness is asked to produce a document and then if he's a document and he's then in such a brusque fashion asked what document that is, I don't think that is appropriate.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I do agree with you that the way in which the request for having access to the document was worded could have been different, and especially in view of the willingness of this expert. It was also the tone, Mr. Ierace. I see that you're -- you said "can I have access to the document?" That's more or less what you said. And certainly I felt that this expert witness is cooperating as good as he can.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: I very much agree with that, Mr. President. I apologise to the witness. It was not intended on my part.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If you would have said, "Sir, would you be willing to give me access to the document," it would have been more -- better, I think.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: But the document can be shown to Mr. Ierace. And then --

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: I notice the time, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Having -- you have looked at it. Yes. Then of course the Defence is also entitled to have a look at the document. No, could you please show it to the Defence, Madam Usher. Mr. Ierace, do you want to do anything with the document or just you --

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Well, perhaps it could be marked at this stage, marked for identification.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Marked for identification. Yes. Could then -- could we do it such a way that it's given to the registrar that she'll mark a copy for identification, that the original will be returned to Dr. Kunjadic. Dr. Kunjadic, we're working here on shifts. That means that we have to stop now because another case will be heard in the afternoon. As you may have noticed, we've not yet finished your testimony. So, therefore, I have to ask you to come back next Monday. Madam Registrar, that would be in the morning again at 9.00, as far as I'm --

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: May I instruct you not to speak with anyone, whoever it is, about the testimony you have given and the testimony you are still about to give in this court. I would like to see you back at 9.00 Monday morning. If there's any need for the parties - because I heard there was some exchange needed - if any assistance of the Chamber is required, it always can be done through the intermediary of the -- one of the legal officers. We'll adjourn until next Monday at 9.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
